newsitem.title: LITHUANIA: Landsbergis aims to seal Lithuania poll victory.
newsitem.headline: Landsbergis aims to seal Lithuania poll victory.

text.p: Lithuanian independence leader Vytautas Landsbergis was expected to snatch back power from his ex-communist rivals, but without an overall majority, after the second round of parliamentary elections.

Landsbergis, the spearhead of Lithuania's bloody 1990-91 bid for independence from the former Soviet Union, was confident the second round would boost his Homeland Union party's first round lead, but did not see a total victory.
"I do not think that we will get an overall majority," he told Reuters as he waited for the results at his party's headquarters in central Vilnius.
First results from Sunday's poll began trickling in by one a.m. local (2300 GMT), with 317 districts of more than 2,036 declared.
Estimates for the Homeland Union's second round performance were ranging between 30 and 38 seats, party officials said.
But the Homeland Union is already committed to a coalition with the Christian Democrats, who won 11 seats in the first round, so the two together were thought likely to be able to form a majority.

A low turnout was taking some of the shine off victory, with just 36.53 percent of people turning out two hours before the polls closed, compared with 48.08 percent at the same stage in the first round on October 20.
The Homeland Union was the major winner in the first round, with 35 of parliament's 141 seats.
That was 25 seats more than the Lithuanian Democratic Labour Party (LDLP), formed from the ashes of the Lithuanian Communist Party, which swept Landsbergis out of office in 1992.

Landsbergis had come to symbolise Lithuania's independence fight, winning admiration for himself and his people when 13 people were killed during an assault on Vilnius TV tower by Soviet troops in January 1991.
But by the time elections came around following year people were weary of the economic chaos that accompanied the break from Moscow and the in-fighting of Landsbergis' Sajudis independence movement.
They turned instead to the familiar faces of the LDLP and their leader Algirdas Brazauskas, who had led an earlier break of Lithuania's Communists from the all-powerful Soviet Communist Party.
The second round of the election works on a majority vote system with 65 seats being contested.
Each seat is being contested by the two candidates who garnered the most votes in their electoral district in the first round for a total of 130 candidates.
Landsbergis and the board chairman of the Homeland Union party, Gediminas Vagnorius, each secured over 50 percent of the vote in their district in the first round and do not have to stand again.
The first round also decided 71 seats on a proportional representation basis, when voters chose from party lists.
Landsbergis is tipped to be chairman of the new parliament and prepare himself to fight Brazauskas for the presidency in February 1998. Vagnorius is set to become the new prime minister.
